pharm: Combination stimulant laxative (sodium picosulfate) plus osmotic laxative (magnesium citrate, formed from magnesium oxide and citric acid)
quick: Two 175 mL bottles (10 mg sodium picosulfate each) as split-dose: 1 evening before, 1 morning of colonoscopy
Clear liquids only the day before; no solids/dairy until after the procedure
No human data; use only if clearly needed (animal studies reassuring)
Active metabolite BHPM undetectable in milk; generally compatible
Contraindicated if CrCl <30 mL/min (magnesium accumulation); caution in mild-moderate impairment
No specific adjustment; elderly may have reduced function
Do not drink alcohol during preparation
Hydration; electrolytes/creatinine/BUN if vomiting, dehydration, or renal risk
summary: Sodium picosulfate combined with magnesium oxide and anhydrous citric acid (CLENPIQ) is a dual-action oral bowel preparation indicated for cleansing the colon before colonoscopy in adults and children 9 years and older. Sodium picosulfate is a stimulant laxative activated by colonic bacteria, while magnesium oxide and citric acid combine in solution to form magnesium citrate, an osmotic laxative that retains water in the gut; together they produce watery diarrhea that empties the colon. It is given as a ready-to-drink, two-bottle split-dose regimen with generous clear-liquid intake. The chief safety concerns are fluid and electrolyte disturbances that can precipitate arrhythmia, seizures, renal impairment, and syncope, so adequate hydration with balanced electrolyte solutions is essential.
indications: Cleansing of the colon as a preparation for colonoscopy in adults
Cleansing of the colon as a preparation for colonoscopy in pediatric patients 9 years of age and older

dosage.c: Colonoscopy prep (adults and children >=9 yr) - Dose 1
dosage.d: One 175 mL bottle (10 mg sodium picosulfate / 3.5 g magnesium oxide / 12 g anhydrous citric acid), ready to drink
dosage.t: Evening before the colonoscopy (e.g., 5:00 PM to 9:00 PM); follow with at least five 8-ounce cups of clear liquids over the next 5 hours
dosage.n: Consume only clear liquids (no solid food or dairy) the day before. If severe bloating, distention, or abdominal pain occurs, delay the second dose until symptoms resolve

dosage.c: Colonoscopy prep (adults and children >=9 yr) - Dose 2
dosage.d: Second 175 mL bottle (same content), ready to drink
dosage.t: Next morning, starting about 5 hours before the colonoscopy; follow with four or more 8-ounce cups of clear liquids, finishing at least 2 hours before the procedure
dosage.n: Two bottles total complete the split-dose regimen. Stop all liquids at least 2 hours before colonoscopy

admin: Ready to drink; do not dilute. One bottle equals one dose; two doses are required for a complete split-dose prep
Correct any fluid and electrolyte abnormalities before administration
Drink a variety of clear liquids after each dose, and include a balanced electrolyte solution (not water alone) to reduce the risk of dehydration and electrolyte shifts

Acceptable clear liquids include water, black coffee or tea, plain jello, clear broth or bouillon, clear pulp-free juices, ginger ale and other sodas, and frozen juice bars; avoid anything colored red or purple
Administer other oral medications at least 1 hour before starting each dose

Tetracycline or fluoroquinolone antibiotics, iron, digoxin, chlorpromazine, and penicillamine should be taken at least 2 hours before and not less than 6 hours after the dose to avoid chelation with magnesium
Do not take other laxatives during the preparation; do not drink alcohol
moa: Sodium picosulfate is hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria to its active metabolite bis-(p-hydroxyphenyl)-pyridyl-2-methane (BHPM), which acts directly on the colonic mucosa to stimulate peristalsis (stimulant laxative effect). Magnesium oxide and citric acid react in solution to form magnesium citrate, an osmotic agent that draws and retains water within the gastrointestinal tract. The combined stimulant and osmotic actions, taken with additional liquids, produce watery diarrhea that cleanses the colon.

absolute: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min) - risk of magnesium accumulation
relative: Mild to moderate renal impairment or use of drugs affecting renal function (diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs)
History of or risk for seizures (including alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, drugs lowering seizure threshold)
Increased risk of arrhythmia (prolonged QT, uncontrolled arrhythmia, recent MI, unstable angina, CHF, cardiomyopathy)
Congestive heart failure (caution when replacing fluids)
Known or suspected inflammatory bowel disease (mucosal ulceration may confound findings)
monitor: Hydration status and orthostatic vital signs
Serum electrolytes, creatinine, and BUN before and after in at-risk patients
Pre- and post-procedure ECG in patients at risk of serious arrhythmia
Blood glucose in pediatric patients (no caloric substrate)

preg: There are no data in pregnant women to establish a drug-associated risk. In animal reproduction studies, oral doses about 1.2 times the recommended human dose (based on body surface area) during organogenesis produced no adverse developmental effects in rats, and published studies with sodium picosulfate showed no fetal harm at much higher multiples. A rabbit study was inadequate due to treatment-related maternal mortality. Use only if clearly needed.
lact: Published data in lactating women show the active metabolite BHPM remained below the limit of detection (1 ng/mL) in breast milk after single and multiple 10 mg/day doses. There are no data on effects on the breastfed infant or on milk production for magnesium oxide or citric acid. Weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against maternal need and any potential infant effects.
renal: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) because magnesium may accumulate in plasma. In mild to moderate impairment, or in patients taking drugs that affect renal function (diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs), there is increased risk of renal injury; emphasize adequate hydration before, during, and after use and consider baseline and post-colonoscopy electrolytes, creatinine, and BUN.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is provided. Sodium picosulfate is minimally absorbed and activated locally by colonic bacteria. Elderly patients are more likely to have decreased hepatic, renal, or cardiac function and may be more susceptible to fluid and electrolyte disturbances.

major: Drugs that increase fluid/electrolyte disturbance risk or that may precipitate seizures, arrhythmia/QT prolongation, syncope, or renal impairment in that setting - use caution
Diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and NSAIDs (increased risk of renal injury and electrolyte shifts)
moderate: Tetracycline and fluoroquinolone antibiotics, iron, digoxin, chlorpromazine, penicillamine (chelation with magnesium reduces their absorption - separate dosing by at least 2 h before and 6 h after)
Drugs that lower the seizure threshold (e.g., tricyclic antidepressants)
minor: Sodium picosulfate did not inhibit major CYP enzymes (1A2, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4/5) or induce CYP1A2, 2B6, or 3A4/5 in vitro
interactions.food: Take only clear liquids during the preparation; no solid food or dairy until after the colonoscopy. Avoid liquids colored red or purple.
interactions.alcohol: Do not drink alcohol during the bowel preparation; alcohol withdrawal also increases seizure risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Prior or concomitant antibiotics may reduce efficacy because colonic bacteria are needed to activate sodium picosulfate to BHPM. Osmotic laxatives may cause colonic mucosal aphthous ulcerations that can mimic or obscure inflammatory bowel disease at colonoscopy. Transient electrolyte shifts (e.g., low potassium, sodium, chloride; high magnesium) may appear on labs around the procedure.

common: Hypermagnesemia (transient, normalizes within about a week)
serious: Colonic mucosal ulceration / ischemic colitis requiring hospitalization
emergency: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures and/or loss of consciousness (associated with electrolyte abnormalities)
Syncope with falls, head injury, or fracture (often within 12 hours of dosing)
Serious cardiac arrhythmias in predisposed patients

monitoring: Adequate hydration before, during, and after each dose
Orthostatic vital signs and symptoms of dehydration (especially with vomiting)
Serum electrolytes, creatinine, and BUN at baseline and post-colonoscopy in renal-impaired or at-risk patients
ECG before and after the procedure in patients at increased arrhythmia risk
Blood glucose in pediatric patients during the prep
counsel: The solution is ready to drink and does not need to be diluted; drink one full bottle per dose and use both bottles as instructed
Drink the recommended clear liquids after each dose - five or more cups after the first, four or more after the second - and include a balanced electrolyte drink, not just water
Eat only clear liquids (no solids or dairy) the day before, do not drink anything red or purple, and do not drink alcohol
Stop all liquids at least 2 hours before the colonoscopy
Get up slowly from lying or sitting to reduce the chance of fainting
Tell your provider if you have a history of fainting, and contact them for significant vomiting, signs of dehydration, confusion, dizziness, fainting, or seizures
If severe bloating or abdominal pain follows the first dose, delay the second dose until it resolves
pk: Watery diarrhea typically begins within a few hours of a dose
Picosulfate Cmax about 2 h after first dose; magnesium Cmax ~1.9 mEq/L at about 10 h
Terminal half-life of sodium picosulfate about 7.4 h (about 7 h in pediatrics)
Purgative effect through the dosing period until the colon is cleared
Store at 25 C (77 F), excursions 15-30 C; do not refrigerate or freeze
pearls: Dual mechanism: sodium picosulfate (bacteria-activated stimulant) plus magnesium citrate (osmotic) formed in situ from magnesium oxide and citric acid
Split-dose administration (evening before plus morning of) gives superior colon cleansing and is the labeled regimen
Recent or concurrent antibiotics can reduce efficacy because gut bacteria are required to activate the prodrug to BHPM
Low caloric load means children should be monitored for hypoglycemia during prep
Encourage balanced electrolyte solutions rather than water alone to limit hyponatremia, syncope, and seizure risk
Avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30) due to magnesium accumulation
missed: This is a single-procedure bowel preparation, not a chronic medication. If a dose is delayed or part of the regimen is missed, contact the prescribing provider or endoscopy unit before the colonoscopy, since incomplete preparation may require rescheduling. Do not double the dose to catch up.
overdose: Taking more than the recommended dose may cause severe electrolyte disturbances, dehydration, and hypovolemia. Monitor for fluid and electrolyte abnormalities and treat symptomatically with rehydration and electrolyte correction.
